newsitem.title: NORWAY: Strong Norway crown lowers inflation forecast.
newsitem.headline: Strong Norway crown lowers inflation forecast.

text.p: Norway's gross domestic product growth is expected to exceed forecasts in 1997 and 1998 and inflation is seen to slow down because of the strong crown, Statistics Norway said on Thursday.
The statistics office, in a quarterly report on key economic indicators, revised up the 1997 GDP growth forecast to 3.1 percent from 3.0 percent in a similar forecast in December.
The 1998 GDP growth forecast was revised up by 0.4 percentage points to 3.0 percent.
"Growth in the Norwegian economy continues to be strong," a statement said.
The growth forecasts were upgraded because of a slightly more expansive government fiscal policy and because of stronger activities in the thriving offshore oil and gas sector, the statement said.

Norway, which pumps over three million barrels of oil per day, is the world's second largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia. A Scandinavian country of 4.3 million people, it keeps only 150,000 barrels for domestic use.

The statistics office reduced the 1997 Consumer Price Index (CPI) growth forecast to 1.8 percent from 2.3 in the December outlook. The inflation forecast for 1998 was revised down by as much as 0.6 percentage points to 1.2 percent.
The changes were attributed to the Norwegian crown, which has firmed by 5.37 percent since last November 5 when the first of three cuts in official interest rates was announced.
The appreciating crown has made imports cheaper, which in turn lowers pressure on prices.

Statistics Norway said it expected the import-weighted crown in 1997 and 1998 to stay five percent above its average level last year. A precondition was that the central bank kept interest rates unchanged.
The finance ministry and the central bank have repeatedly said, however, that the crown will gradually be weakened to its previous levels.
Neither the ministry nor the bank have said how this might be done, given strong market pressure on the currency.

The bank cut official interest rates for the second time in two days on January 10 only to see the oil-backed currency power to new peaks. Buckling under market pressure, it then announced a temporary halt to its massive but fruitless intervention.

The crown on Thursday stood at about 95.80 on the inverse ECU index of European currencies, a theoretical basket used by the bank to monitor the strength of the currency. Against the mark, the crown held its ground at about 3.92 crowns.
Statistics Norway said the 1997 current account surplus was now seen rising to 73.9 billion crowns from a forecast 71.2 billion in December thanks to the petroleum production.

This year's mainland GDP growth, which excludes the North Sea oil and gas sector, was kept unchanged at 2.7 percent, but grow by 0.4 percentage points to 2.7 percent in 1998 compared with the previous forecast.
Unemployment was expected to grow to 4.5 percent this year compared with a previous forecast of 4.0 percent. In January, the jobless rate was 4.1 percent.
